description: Code that waits: callbacks, promises, and the async/await that tames them.

screens.body:
Most JavaScript runs top to bottom, one line after another. But some things take time: loading data, waiting a second, reading a file.

JavaScript doesn't freeze while waiting — it starts the slow job, keeps running the rest of your code, and handles the result when it's ready. That's asynchronous code.

options: It keeps running other code and handles the result when it arrives
It freezes the whole page until the data loads
It skips the slow job entirely
check.question: When JavaScript starts a slow job (like loading data), what does it do?

screens.heading: Some code has to wait
screens.keyPoint: Async = start the slow job, handle the result later.

screens.body:
The oldest way to handle "later": hand JavaScript a function (a callback) to run when the job finishes.

setTimeout says "run this function after 1000 milliseconds." The rest of your code doesn't wait — "done waiting" prints a second later.

options: It runs after about 1 second, while other code continues
check.question: What does setTimeout(() => console.log("hi"), 1000) do?

screens.heading: Callbacks: "call me when you're done"
screens.keyPoint: A callback is a function you hand over to run later.

screens.body:
Callbacks work, but stacking them gets ugly fast: each step nests inside the previous one, drifting rightward into a pyramid.

Developers called this "callback hell" — hard to read, harder to debug. JavaScript needed a cleaner way to say "do this, then that."

options: Deeply nested callbacks that are hard to read
Too many functions in one file
check.question: What is "callback hell"?

screens.heading: Too many callbacks gets messy
screens.keyPoint: Nested callbacks become unreadable — hence promises.

screens.body:
A promise is a receipt for a value that isn't ready yet. It starts as pending, then settles as fulfilled (with the value) or rejected (with an error).

You create one with new Promise, and it takes a function with resolve ("here's the value") and reject ("something broke").

check.question: A promise whose value hasn't arrived yet is in what state?

screens.heading: Promises: receipts for future values

screens.body:
To use the future value, chain .then(): it runs your function when the promise fulfills, receiving the value.

You can chain multiple .thens — each one gets the previous step's result. The code reads top to bottom again, no nesting pyramid.

check.question: order.then(food => console.log("Got: " + food)) with order resolving to "pizza" — what prints?

screens.heading: .then() runs when it's ready
screens.keyPoint: .then() receives the value when the promise fulfills.

screens.body:
Promises can fail: bad network, missing file, wrong password. Add .catch() at the end of the chain to handle rejections in one place.

Without .catch(), a rejection crashes or silently dies. Always end promise chains with error handling — future you will be grateful.

check.question: A promise might reject. What's the fix?

screens.heading: Handling failures with .catch()
screens.keyPoint: Always handle rejections — end chains with .catch().

screens.body:
async/await is the modern way: mark a function async, then use await to pause that function until a promise settles. The code reads like normal top-to-bottom code.

await only works inside async functions. An async function always returns a promise — so callers can still .then() or await it.

options: Pauses until the promise settles, then continues
check.question: What does await do inside an async function?

screens.heading: async/await: waiting, the readable way
screens.keyPoint: await pauses one function — not the whole program.
